title: Euclidean Radon transform and filtered backprojection

items.title: The Euclidean Radon transform on R²

references.title: Mikko Salo, RICAM lecture notes v1, §2.1: Radon transform in R²
references.locator: §2.1, pp. 4–7: line parameterization, Fourier convention, and full-angle backprojection.

references.title: Frank Natterer, X-ray Tomography, in Inverse Problems and Imaging
references.locator: §2.1, pp. 18–20: Radon transform, Fourier slice theorem, and inversion; §3.1, pp. 26–28: filtered-backprojection discretization.

items.statement:
Write $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth functions of compact support on the Euclidean plane. For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $n=1$ or $2$, use the compact-support Riemann Fourier transform
$$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$
For $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in S^1:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|=1\}$ put $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$. The line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x\cdot\theta=s\}$. Its **Euclidean Radon transform** is
$$Rf(\theta,s):=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt,\qquad f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C),\ (\theta,s)\in S^1\times\mathbb R.$$
The line integral is a compact-support Riemann integral.
The full data set uses every oriented normal $\theta\in S^1$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$; the same unoriented line is represented by $(\theta,s)$ and $(-\theta,-s)$.
For a one-dimensional function $h$ with integrable Fourier transform, define
$$|D_s|h(s):=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\,\widehat h(\sigma)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma.$$
For $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ define the Riesz potential notation used here by
$$|D|^{-1}f(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\frac{\widehat f(\xi)}{2\pi|\xi|}\,d\xi.$$
The quotient in the last integral is assigned value $0$ at $\xi=0$. These integrals are absolutely convergent on the stated classes: compact-support integration by parts gives rapid decay of $\widehat f$ and $\widehat h$, while $\widehat f$ is bounded near $0$ and $|\xi|^{-1}$ is locally integrable in two dimensions. Here the multiplier for $|D_s|$ is $2\pi|\sigma|$, corresponding to the $e^{-2\pi i s\sigma}$ Fourier convention.

items.title: The Fourier-slice identity for the Euclidean Radon transform

references.title: Mikko Salo, RICAM lecture notes v1, §2.1: Radon transform in R²
references.locator: §2.1, pp. 4–7: Fourier-slice theorem and its Fubini proof.

references.title: Frank Natterer, X-ray Tomography, in Inverse Problems and Imaging
references.locator: §2.1, pp. 18–20, Theorem 2.1: projection-slice theorem and line-coordinate proof.

items.statement:
For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$, every unit normal $\theta\in S^1$, and every $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, the compact-support Fourier transform of the line data in the offset variable equals the restriction of the two-dimensional Fourier transform to the line in frequency space with direction $\theta$:
$$\widehat{Rf}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta).$$

items.title: The Euclidean Radon normal operator and inversion formula

references.title: Mikko Salo, RICAM lecture notes v1, §2.1: Radon transform in R²
references.locator: §2.1, pp. 4–7: normal operator, polar-coordinate calculation, and filtered-backprojection formula.

references.title: Frank Natterer, X-ray Tomography, in Inverse Problems and Imaging
references.locator: §2.1, pp. 18–20, Theorems 2.1–2.2 and formula (7): slice theorem and two-dimensional inversion formula.

items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mu$ be the polar surface measure on $S^1$, defined on Borel $E\subseteq S^1$ by
$$\mu(E):=2\lambda_2\bigl(\{r\theta:\theta\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}\bigr),$$
where $\lambda_2$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^2$. For continuous $g:S^1\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ for which the integral exists, define its **backprojection** by
$$R^*g(x):=\int_{S^1}g(\theta,x\cdot\theta)\,d\mu(\theta).$$
For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^2$, the normal-operator and filtered-backprojection identities hold:
$$R^*Rf(x)=4\pi|D|^{-1}f(x),\qquad f(x)=\frac1{4\pi}R^*|D_s|Rf(x),$$
with $|D|^{-1}$ and $|D_s|$ as defined for the compact-support Fourier convention in the Euclidean Radon transform definition.

items.title: Complete-data filtered backprojection

references.title: Mikko Salo, RICAM lecture notes v1, §2.1: Radon transform in R²
Frank Natterer, X-ray Tomography, in Inverse Problems and Imaging
references.locator: §3.1, pp. 26–28: filtering and backprojection steps and their finite-sampling context.

items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and let $\mu$ be the polar surface measure on $S^1$, with $\mu(E)=2\lambda_2(\{r\theta:\theta\in E,\ 0<r\le1\})$ for Borel $E\subseteq S^1$. The **complete-data filtered-backprojection procedure** takes as input the exact full sinogram $g=Rf$ of some $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$; all oriented normals $\theta\in S^1$ and all offsets $s\in\mathbb R$ are supplied. It returns the function $f_{\mathrm{FBP}}:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb C$ defined by
$$f_{\mathrm{FBP}}(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^1}q(\theta,x\cdot\theta)\,d\mu(\theta),$$
where the filter output is
$$q(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\,\widehat{g(\theta,\cdot)}(\sigma)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma.$$
The exact instructions are: (1) for each $\theta$, take the one-dimensional Fourier transform of $g(\theta,\cdot)$ with the negative-sign $2\pi$ convention; (2) multiply that transform by the declared ramp filter $2\pi|\sigma|$ and take its inverse Fourier integral to form $q(\theta,\cdot)$; (3) evaluate $q(\theta,\cdot)$ at $s=x\cdot\theta$ and integrate over the full polar surface measure in $\theta$; (4) divide by $4\pi$. For this input class the slice identity and Schwartz decay make the filter integral absolutely convergent and the backprojection integral well defined. This definition specifies the continuous full-data procedure; it gives no guarantee for finitely sampled, truncated, or noisy measurements. Exact recovery on the stated class is proved by the normal-operator theorem.

title: Euclidean Radon transform and filtered backprojection — Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A smooth radial phantom and its sinogram
items.statement:
Define $\eta(u)=0$ for $u\le0$ and $\eta(u)=e^{-1/u}$ for $u>0$, and put $f(x)=\eta(1-|x|^2)$ on $\mathbb R^2$. This is a nonzero, smooth, compactly supported radial phantom. Its Euclidean Radon transform is independent of $\theta$ and is
$$Rf(\theta,s)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt{1-s^2}}^{\sqrt{1-s^2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{1-s^2-t^2}\right)\,dt,&|s|<1,\\[1.2ex]0,&|s|\ge1.\end{cases}$$

items.title: A point source as a distributional Radon limit
items.statement:
Let $\eta(u)=0$ for $u\le0$ and $\eta(u)=e^{-1/u}$ for $u>0$, set $\psi(x)=\eta(1-|x|^2)$ on $\mathbb R^2$, let $J=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\psi(x)\,dx$, and define $\phi=J^{-1}\psi$. For $\varepsilon>0$ put $\phi_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-2}\phi(x/\varepsilon)$. The functions $\phi_\varepsilon$ are radial smooth unit-mass point-source approximations. For $\rho(s)=\int_{\mathbb R}\phi(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$, which is independent of $\theta$, their full line data satisfy
$$R\phi_\varepsilon(\theta,s)=\varepsilon^{-1}\rho(s/\varepsilon).$$
For each fixed $\theta\in S^1$ and every test function $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$, the offset distributions converge to the point mass:
$$\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_{\mathbb R}R\phi_\varepsilon(\theta,s)h(s)\,ds=h(0).$$
Thus the point-source sinogram is $\delta_0(s)$ in the offset variable, for every line normal.

items.title: A finite complete-angle filtered-backprojection calculation

references.title: Frank Natterer, X-ray Tomography, in Inverse Problems and Imaging
references.locator: §3.1, pp. 26–28: filtering and angular backprojection quadrature for sampled data.

items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice for the continuous backprojection convention. As a finite-grid illustration, take eight equally spaced full-circle directions $\theta_j=(\cos(2\pi j/8),\sin(2\pi j/8))$, $j=0,\ldots,7$, four detector offsets $s_m=m-2$ for $m=0,1,2,3$, detector spacing $\Delta s=1$, and the synthetic row $G_j=(0,0,1,0)$ at every direction. Apply the length-four radix-two FFT to each row, multiply frequency $k$ by the declared sampled ramp $\lambda_k=2\pi\min(k,4-k)/4$, and invert the finite transform. Each filtered row is $Q=(0,-\pi/4,\pi/2,-\pi/4)$. With the eight-point trapezoidal angular rule of weight $\Delta\theta=\pi/4$, the one-pixel backprojection at $x=0$ is
$$\widetilde f_h(0)=\frac1{4\pi}\Delta\theta\sum_{j=0}^7Q_j[2]=\frac\pi4.$$
This is the exact output of the specified finite computation. The array is a synthetic discrete sinogram; no claim is made that the finite detector or angle grid exactly represents a continuous phantom or that this output converges to one. The continuous theorem assumes full continuous data and makes no finite-sampling, truncation, or noise guarantee.
